html:
The Ecloga, Greek for "selection", is a short Byzantine law book issued in the names of Leo III and his son Constantine V, in 726 or, as many now think, 741. It boiled down the huge Corpus Juris Civilis of Justinian I, which was in Latin and far too long for judges to use, into one handy book in Greek.

It covered family law, inheritance, contracts and crimes. Its preface speaks of equal justice for rich and poor, and it shows Christian ideas at work: it strengthened the rights of wives and children and limited divorce. It also replaced the death penalty for many crimes with mutilation, such as cutting off the nose or a hand, which was seen as more merciful because it left time to repent.

The Ecloga was used for more than a century. The Macedonian emperors replaced it in the 880s, partly to erase the work of the iconoclast emperors, and later with the Basilika. Slavic peoples translated and adapted it.
